topics.title: Official chapter 4 — Test Analysis and Design

studyGuide.sectionTitle: Chapter keywords: explain, distinguish and exemplify

elements.text: These are original plain-language explanations, not quotations from the official glossary. For each term, give a new example and explain its difference from a neighboring term. Use the official glossary with the CTFL syllabus context for authoritative wording.

rows: Shared conditions a story or feature must satisfy to be accepted; make expected positive and negative behavior clear.
Collaboratively derive acceptance examples before implementation and use them to guide the work.
A systematic way to derive tests from the required behavior rather than implementation structure.
Derive cases around the limits of ordered equivalence partitions, using the specified 2-value or 3-value criterion.
Exercised control-flow branches divided by the total modeled branches, expressed as a percentage.
Use a maintained list of test conditions to guide checks while allowing context-specific execution.
Develop shared testable understanding through contributions from business, development and testing perspectives.
The proportion of the selected kind of coverage items exercised, rather than a general proof of correctness.
A distinct element to be exercised under a criterion, such as a partition, feasible rule, transition, statement or branch.
Derive cases from feasible combinations of conditions and their associated actions.
Divide a domain into groups expected to be treated alike and choose representative values from each relevant group.
Target likely mistakes using experience of the application, domain and previous defects.
Derive tests primarily from people's knowledge and practical experience of likely failures.
Integrate learning, design and execution, with observations influencing subsequent tests.
Derive event sequences from a model of states and valid or invalid transitions.
Executed executable statements divided by total executable statements, expressed as a percentage.
A repeatable method for selecting conditions, cases, data and coverage items.
A method for deriving cases from the internal structure of the test object.

elements.text: Official exam weighting: 11/40 questions (27.5%). Work in short topic blocks; retrieve before rereading. The chapter quiz contains 28 original questions across all objectives of this chapter. Revisit high-confidence errors with Smart Review and use the full official chapter and keywords to check completeness.
K3 application objectives here: FL-4.2.1, FL-4.2.2, FL-4.2.3, FL-4.2.4, FL-4.5.3. Practise them on paper with the Try first exercises until you can solve unseen examples without hints.

elements.description: Black-box techniques model specified behavior; white-box techniques analyze internal structure; experience-based techniques exploit tester knowledge. They complement each other rather than competing for a universal best choice.

elements.text: Worked example: A decision table comes from business rules; branch tests come from control flow; error guessing comes from prior failures.
Close the notes: Classify a proposed technique by the basis used to derive tests.

elements.description: Identify non-empty, non-overlapping groups expected to be treated alike. Cover valid and invalid partitions. Each Choice for multiple inputs covers every partition of each input, not every combination.

elements.text: Worked example: An integer quota accepts 10 through 50 inclusive: below 10, 10–50 and above 50 are three partitions. Values 9, 30 and 51 cover all three.

elements.title: Build partitions from behavior
items: Identify the input domain and each distinct specified behavior. Include feasible invalid inputs.
Choose one representative per non-empty partition for each input. Record the expected outcome, not just the value.
For multiple inputs, distinguish Each Choice coverage from all combinations. Count covered partitions over all identified partitions.

elements.title: Delivery quantity and service
elements.prompt: Delivery quantity is an integer: 1–20 is accepted; smaller and larger quantities are rejected. Service is standard or express; every other service value is rejected. Derive all partitions. Calculate Each Choice coverage for tests (5, standard) and (12, express). Then add the fewest tests that reach 100%, with at most one invalid value per test.
elements.solution: Quantity has three partitions (≤0, 1–20, ≥21); service has three (standard, express, other): six in total. The two tests cover 1–20, standard and express: 3/6 = 50%. Add (0, standard), (21, express) and (5, other). Each new test contains one invalid value, so a rejection can be traced to its cause, and coverage becomes 6/6 = 100%. Each Choice coverage does not test every combination.

elements.text: Close the notes: Derive partitions before choosing representatives and calculate covered / total partitions.

elements.description: Start with the feasible input domain and every ordered partition, including invalid partitions. List each finite minimum and maximum. The union of these boundary values is the 2-value coverage set. For 3-value coverage add both immediate neighbors of every boundary value, keep only feasible inputs and deduplicate. An unbounded integer domain with accepted L through U has finite boundaries L-1,L,U,U+1; full 3-value coverage normally also needs L-2,L+1,U-1,U+2. A bounded domain can add outer endpoints and their feasible neighbors; close boundaries can overlap.

elements.text: Worked example: For the domain of all integers with accepted 10–50, partitions are x<10, 10–50 and x>50. Finite boundary values are 9,10,50,51. Their 3-value neighborhoods unite to 8,9,10,11,49,50,51,52. If the feasible domain instead starts at zero, add outer boundary 0 to the 2-value set and 0,1 to the 3-value set. Negative values are then infeasible, not extra invalid test inputs.

elements.title: Derive coverage before choosing test data
items: State the feasible domain and precision. A possible but rejected input is invalid; a value outside the domain is infeasible.
Identify every ordered equivalence partition, including invalid ones. List each finite minimum and maximum; an unbounded end has no finite extreme.
For 2-value BVA, combine the boundary values of all partitions and remove duplicates. For 3-value BVA, add the immediate predecessor and successor of each boundary value when feasible.
Remove duplicates when partition limits or neighborhoods overlap. Calculate coverage using this derived item set rather than a fixed multiplier.

elements.text: Compared with the worked example above, a non-negative domain adds the finite minimum 0, and −1 is infeasible. A singleton partition has the same minimum and maximum, so neighborhoods overlap. No fixed six-value or eight-value shortcut is safe: the domain, partitions and requested scope determine the set.

elements.title: Price field with two decimals
elements.prompt: A price field accepts 0.01 to 99.99 in steps of 0.01. Negative values cannot be entered. 0.00 and every value from 100.00 upward can be entered but are rejected; there is no upper input limit. Identify the partitions, then list the 2-value and 3-value BVA sets.
elements.solution: Partitions: {0.00} invalid, 0.01–99.99 valid, ≥100.00 invalid. The upper invalid partition has no finite maximum. 2-value set: 0.00, 0.01, 99.99, 100.00 (4 values). 3-value set: 0.00, 0.01, 0.02, 99.98, 99.99, 100.00, 100.01 (7 values). −0.01 is infeasible, and overlapping neighbors are counted once.

elements.text: Close the notes: Declare the feasible domain, derive every partition and its extrema, then form both coverage unions. Explain why valid endpoints alone omit invalid-partition boundaries.

items.label: ISTQB clarification: derive BVA from the domain and all partition boundaries

elements.description: Represent condition combinations as rules and associate actions. Remove infeasible rules; merge rules with identical outcomes when a condition is irrelevant. Coverage counts exercised feasible rules, not individual conditions.

elements.text: Worked example: A discount needs membership AND a qualifying basket. With two independent booleans, four feasible combinations exist; only true/true earns the discount.

For the rule Member AND Qualifying basket, the two conditions give 2×2 = 4 combinations, so the full table has four columns. A test for member=false, qualifying=false exercises R4 and expects no discount. Testing R1 twice still covers only one distinct rule.

rows: The condition is satisfied / not satisfied.
The condition is irrelevant to the outcome of this rule.
The condition is infeasible for this rule. It is not the same as irrelevant.
Perform the action / do not perform it.

elements.text: When membership is false, the basket condition is irrelevant, so the two full-table columns merge into Reduced R3. Coverage counts the feasible rule columns of the table actually under test; infeasible columns are excluded. Full minimization algorithms are outside CTFL scope.

elements.title: Account creation rules
elements.prompt: An account is created if the applicant is registered AND (is 18 or older OR has parental consent). Conditions in order: registered, adult, consent. Build the full table, then a reduced table. Which reduced rules do tests (T,T,F) and (F,F,F) cover, and what coverage do they achieve?
elements.solution: Full table: 2³ = 8 rules. An account is created only for (T,T,T), (T,T,F) and (T,F,T). Reduced table, four rules: not registered (others -) → no account; registered and adult (consent -) → create; registered, not adult, consent → create; registered, not adult, no consent → no account. (T,T,F) exercises the registered-and-adult rule and (F,F,F) the not-registered rule: 2/4 = 50%. Add (T,F,T) and (T,F,F) to reach 100% of the reduced table.

elements.text: Close the notes: Construct the full table before minimizing it and keep impossible combinations separate.

elements.description: Model states and event-triggered transitions, including guards and actions. State coverage can miss transitions. All valid transition coverage exercises each modeled valid transition. All transitions coverage adds attempted invalid transitions from the state table; isolate one invalid transition per test to avoid defect masking. All transitions coverage subsumes valid transitions coverage, which subsumes all states coverage.

elements.text: Worked example: Draft → Submitted → Approved → Draft visits three states but a separate Submitted → Draft rejection transition remains untested.

Original guarded example: states Locked and Unlocked. Label syntax is event [guard] / action. From Locked, badge [valid] / release goes to Unlocked; badge [not valid] / recordFailure is a valid self-loop back to Locked. From Unlocked, timeout / engage returns to Locked.
The syllabus convention leaves invalid transitions as empty cells; Invalid is written here for readability.

Start Locked: badge(valid), timeout, badge(not valid) covers all three valid transitions, including the self-loop. The rejected badge in Locked is a modeled valid transition, not an invalid transition. The three Invalid cells need separate attempted-event tests if all-transitions coverage is requested; isolate one invalid attempt per test to limit defect masking.

elements.title: Coverage of a short test
elements.prompt: Using the table above, one test starts Locked and runs badge(valid), then timeout. Calculate all-states, valid-transitions and all-transitions coverage.
elements.solution: States: Locked and Unlocked are both visited, 2/2 = 100%. Valid transitions: release and engage are exercised, but the recordFailure self-loop is not: 2/3 ≈ 67%. All transitions (3 valid + 3 invalid table cells): 2/6 ≈ 33%. Full state coverage does not imply full transition coverage.

elements.title: Invalid transitions
elements.prompt: Using the table above, design one test for each Invalid cell. Start each test Locked, name its setup sequence and make exactly one invalid attempt. Do not chain invalid events.
elements.solution: (1) No setup; attempt timeout in Locked. (2) badge(valid) to reach Unlocked; attempt badge(valid). (3) badge(valid) to reach Unlocked; attempt badge(not valid). These cover the three invalid cells separately. With the valid-transition sequence above they exercise all six table cells. The state model does not specify error messages: take the expected rejection behavior from the requirements, and do not assume an invalid attempt changes state.

elements.text: Close the notes: Trace the events from the specified initial state and distinguish states from transitions.

elements.description: Statement coverage is executed executable statements divided by total executable statements. Full statement coverage says nothing certain about untested decision outcomes or missing requirements.

elements.text: Trace model: S1 sets fee=0; decision D tests premium; its true outcome executes S2, which sets fee=5; both paths reach S3, which returns fee. The executable statements are S1, D, S2 and S3 (the decision itself counts as a statement). The control-flow graph has four branches: S1→D, D→S2 (true), D→S3 (false) and S2→S3.

elements.title: One test, two coverage measures
elements.prompt: The only test uses premium=true. Calculate statement coverage and branch coverage for the model above. Which branch is not exercised?
elements.solution: Statements: S1, D, S2 and S3 all execute, 4/4 = 100%. Branches: S1→D, D→S2 and S2→S3 execute, 3/4 = 75%. D→S3 (premium=false) is not exercised. 100% statement coverage does not imply 100% branch coverage. CTFL branch coverage counts every branch in the graph, conditional and unconditional, not only the decision outcomes.

elements.text: Recap example: An if-without-else can execute every statement when true while never testing its false branch.
Close the notes: Compute statement coverage and explain what 100% does not establish.

elements.description: Branch coverage counts exercised control-flow branches. Full branch coverage subsumes full statement coverage, but not the reverse; neither implies all paths or correct requirements.

elements.title: Branches versus paths
elements.prompt: Decision X tests x>0: true executes A, false executes B. Both continue to decision Y, which tests y>0: true executes C, false executes D. Both end at End. The control-flow graph has eight branches: X→A, X→B, A→Y, B→Y, Y→C, Y→D, C→End, D→End. What branch coverage do tests (1,1) and (−1,−1) achieve? Which routes through the code are never executed?
elements.solution: (1,1) exercises X→A, A→Y, Y→C, C→End; (−1,−1) exercises X→B, B→Y, Y→D, D→End: 8/8 = 100% branch coverage, so every statement also executes. The routes A-then-D and B-then-C are never executed. Full branch coverage does not mean every path has run; path testing is outside CTFL scope. Neither result proves the specified behavior is correct.

elements.text: Recap example: Running both outcomes of each if covers branches, but not necessarily every combination of outcomes through the program.
Close the notes: Explain why all branches does not mean all paths.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: FL-4.3.3 · Value of white-box testing · K2

elements.description: Structural coverage supplies objective evidence and can reveal gaps in behavior-based testing. It cannot identify an omitted requirement simply because all implemented code is exercised.

elements.text: Worked example: A coverage tool reports 100% for a calculator that lacks a required tax rule. The missing rule still needs specification-based tests.
Close the notes: What defect can remain when the implemented structure has full coverage?

elements.description: Use experience of errors, defects, failures and the application domain to target likely mistakes. Fault attacks organize likely defect types and corresponding tests.

elements.text: Worked example: Past timezone failures motivate trying a date across a daylight-saving transition.
Close the notes: Distinguish a hypothesis about likely mistakes from a formal structural coverage target.

elements.description: Learning, test design and execution influence each other during exploration. A timeboxed session can use a charter, notes, coverage observations and a debrief; exploration is not unrecorded random clicking.

elements.text: Worked example: A tester investigates interrupted checkout, follows a surprising result and records observations within a session charter.
Close the notes: Write a focused charter and name the evidence you would record.

elements.description: Use a list of conditions derived from experience and needs to guide checks. Keep it relevant and update it with findings. Broad items permit varied execution, but vague or stale lists can miss defects.

elements.text: Worked example: An accessibility checklist prompts keyboard navigation checks across screens without prescribing every click.
Close the notes: How would a checklist guide testing without becoming a detailed script?

elements.description: Business, development and testing perspectives refine a story together. The card starts a conversation and confirmation examples clarify intent. INVEST asks for independent, negotiable, valuable, estimable, small and testable stories.

elements.text: Worked example: A tester asks what happens when a booking fails, helping turn a vague story into testable behavior.
Close the notes: Use the three perspectives to resolve one ambiguity in a story.

elements.description: Acceptance criteria set shared, unambiguous conditions for accepting a story and include positive and negative behavior. They may be scenario-oriented or rule-oriented.

elements.text: Worked example: Given a locked account, when correct credentials are entered, then access remains denied is scenario-oriented; a list of locking rules is rule-oriented.
Close the notes: Express the same acceptance condition in both formats.

elements.description: Discuss the story and criteria before implementation; derive stakeholder-readable tests for its characteristics. Include positive, negative and relevant non-functional cases without inventing unrelated scope. Agree concrete examples before implementation, then use their expected results to guide the work.

elements.text: Worked example: For free delivery on baskets of at least EUR 60, EUR 60 gets free delivery and EUR 59 does not. Agree these examples before coding.

elements.title: Derive acceptance cases before implementation
items: Clarify the story and acceptance criteria with business, development and testing perspectives; resolve ambiguity before inventing expected results.
Derive a normal case, negative cases and any specified non-functional case. State preconditions, inputs and observable postconditions.
Trace each case to a criterion, remove duplicates and avoid adding behavior beyond the story. Automation is optional.

elements.title: Order cancellation story
elements.prompt: A signed-in customer may cancel their own Pending order; cancellation sets it to Cancelled and restores its reserved stock once. Shipped orders reject cancellation without changing stock. Write two acceptance cases. What does a second cancellation request require you to clarify?
elements.solution: Given a Pending order with 2 reserved units and available stock 8, when its customer cancels, then the status is Cancelled and stock is 10. Given a Shipped order and stock 8, when its customer attempts cancellation, then cancellation is rejected, the status stays Shipped and stock stays 8. The story does not define the response to a repeated request for a Cancelled order: clarify it collaboratively while keeping the once-only stock rule. Do not invent a response code or latency requirement.

elements.text: Close the notes: Derive tests that follow exactly the story's acceptance rules.
Attempt these after studying the chapter, without looking at the keyword table. Explain each answer in your own words, then open the solution.

elements.title: Coverage item versus coverage
elements.prompt: For an age field you identify 3 equivalence partitions and your tests exercise 2 of them. What are the coverage items, and what is the coverage?
elements.solution: The 3 partitions are the coverage items, derived from the test conditions. Coverage is 2/3 ≈ 67%. Always state the items and the denominator with a coverage figure.

elements.title: Classify the techniques
elements.prompt: Classify: equivalence partitioning, branch testing, error guessing, decision table testing, checklist-based testing, statement testing, exploratory testing, state transition testing.
elements.solution: Black-box: equivalence partitioning, decision table testing, state transition testing. White-box: statement testing, branch testing. Experience-based: error guessing, exploratory testing, checklist-based testing.

elements.title: Which experience-based technique?
elements.prompt: Name the technique in each case. (1) A tester designs, executes and evaluates tests at the same time within a time-boxed charter. (2) A tester anticipates likely mistakes from past failures, such as empty input or division by zero. (3) A tester follows a list of questions derived from experience and standards.
elements.solution: (1) Exploratory testing, here session-based. (2) Error guessing. (3) Checklist-based testing.

elements.title: Acceptance criteria versus ATDD
elements.prompt: A story states: “Orders of at least EUR 60 ship free.” The team agrees examples (EUR 60 free, EUR 59.99 charged) and writes tests from them before coding. Which part is the acceptance criterion and which is ATDD?
elements.solution: “Orders of at least EUR 60 ship free” is an acceptance criterion: a condition the story must meet. Agreeing examples and deriving tests before implementation is acceptance test-driven development, a collaboration-based test approach.

examPitfalls.title: FL-4.1.1 · Technique families
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Technique families are determined by which tool executes the tests rather than the test basis.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Black-box techniques model specified behavior; white-box techniques analyze internal structure; experience-based techniques exploit tester knowledge. They complement each other rather than competing for a universal best choice. Self-check: Classify a proposed technique by the basis used to derive tests.

examPitfalls.title: FL-4.2.1 · Equivalence partitioning
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Valid partitions are sufficient, and Each Choice means all combinations of input partitions.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Identify non-empty, non-overlapping groups expected to be treated alike. Cover valid and invalid partitions. Each Choice for multiple inputs covers every partition of each input, not every combination. Self-check: Derive partitions before choosing representatives and calculate covered / total partitions.

examPitfalls.title: FL-4.2.2 · Boundary value analysis
examPitfalls.trapDescription: A midpoint can replace an immediate boundary neighbor, or 2-value and 3-value sets are identical.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Start with the feasible input domain and every ordered partition, including invalid partitions. List each finite minimum and maximum. The union of these boundary values is the 2-value coverage set. For 3-value coverage add both immediate neighbors of every boundary value, keep only feasible inputs and deduplicate. An unbounded integer domain with accepted L through U has finite boundaries L-1,L,U,U+1; full 3-value coverage normally also needs L-2,L+1,U-1,U+2. A bounded domain can add outer endpoints and their feasible neighbors; close boundaries can overlap. Self-check: Declare the feasible domain, derive every partition and its extrema, then form both coverage unions. Explain why valid endpoints alone omit invalid-partition boundaries.

examPitfalls.title: FL-4.2.3 · Decision tables
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Rule coverage counts individual conditions or test executions instead of distinct feasible rules.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Represent condition combinations as rules and associate actions. Remove infeasible rules; merge rules with identical outcomes when a condition is irrelevant. Coverage counts exercised feasible rules, not individual conditions. Self-check: Construct the full table before minimizing it and keep impossible combinations separate.

examPitfalls.title: FL-4.2.4 · State transitions
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Visiting every state guarantees that every transition and invalid event has been checked.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Model states and event-triggered transitions, including guards and actions. State coverage can miss transitions. All valid transition coverage exercises each modeled valid transition. All transitions coverage adds attempted invalid transitions from the state table; isolate one invalid transition per test to avoid defect masking. All transitions coverage subsumes valid transitions coverage, which subsumes all states coverage. Self-check: Trace the events from the specified initial state and distinguish states from transitions.

examPitfalls.title: FL-4.3.1 · Statement testing
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Executing every statement guarantees every decision outcome has been exercised.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Statement coverage is executed executable statements divided by total executable statements. Full statement coverage says nothing certain about untested decision outcomes or missing requirements. Self-check: Compute statement coverage and explain what 100% does not establish.

examPitfalls.title: FL-4.3.2 · Branch testing
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Full branch coverage guarantees every possible execution path and correct business behavior.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Branch coverage counts exercised control-flow branches. Full branch coverage subsumes full statement coverage, but not the reverse; neither implies all paths or correct requirements. Self-check: Explain why all branches does not mean all paths.

examPitfalls.title: FL-4.3.3 · Value of white-box testing
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Structural coverage detects a required feature even when its implementation is entirely missing.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Structural coverage supplies objective evidence and can reveal gaps in behavior-based testing. It cannot identify an omitted requirement simply because all implemented code is exercised. Self-check: What defect can remain when the implemented structure has full coverage?

examPitfalls.title: FL-4.4.1 · Error guessing
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Error guessing means selecting arbitrary inputs without a hypothesis about likely faults.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Use experience of errors, defects, failures and the application domain to target likely mistakes. Fault attacks organize likely defect types and corresponding tests. Self-check: Distinguish a hypothesis about likely mistakes from a formal structural coverage target.

examPitfalls.title: FL-4.4.2 · Exploratory testing
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Exploratory testing prohibits planning, evidence, a mission or a debrief.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Learning, test design and execution influence each other during exploration. A timeboxed session can use a charter, notes, coverage observations and a debrief; exploration is not unrecorded random clicking. Self-check: Write a focused charter and name the evidence you would record.

examPitfalls.title: FL-4.4.3 · Checklist-based testing
examPitfalls.trapDescription: A completed checklist guarantees completeness and should never be updated.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Use a list of conditions derived from experience and needs to guide checks. Keep it relevant and update it with findings. Broad items permit varied execution, but vague or stale lists can miss defects. Self-check: How would a checklist guide testing without becoming a detailed script?

examPitfalls.title: FL-4.5.1 · Collaborative user stories
examPitfalls.trapDescription: A user story is a fixed contract whose examples should be written by one discipline alone.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Business, development and testing perspectives refine a story together. The card starts a conversation and confirmation examples clarify intent. INVEST asks for independent, negotiable, valuable, estimable, small and testable stories. Self-check: Use the three perspectives to resolve one ambiguity in a story.

examPitfalls.title: FL-4.5.2 · Acceptance criteria
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Acceptance criteria must use Given/When/Then and cannot be expressed as clear rules.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Acceptance criteria set shared, unambiguous conditions for accepting a story and include positive and negative behavior. They may be scenario-oriented or rule-oriented. Self-check: Express the same acceptance condition in both formats.

examPitfalls.title: FL-4.5.3 · Acceptance test-driven development
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Acceptance examples may invent unrelated behavior, or test-first means writing tests after the feature is complete.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Discuss the story and criteria before implementation; derive stakeholder-readable tests for its characteristics. Include positive, negative and relevant non-functional cases without inventing unrelated scope. Agree concrete examples before implementation, then use their expected results to guide the work. Self-check: Derive tests that follow exactly the story's acceptance rules.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Tests are derived from documented business rules without using source code. Which family is this?
practiceQuiz.rationale: A behavioral specification is a black-box basis. White-box uses internal structure; experience-based uses tester knowledge; configuration management controls artifacts.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A tester uses control-flow branches to derive cases. Which family is this?
practiceQuiz.rationale: Internal control flow is a white-box basis. The alternatives use specified behavior, experience or collaboration rather than structure.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: An integer quantity accepts 5–20 inclusive and rejects other integers. Which set covers the three partitions?
practiceQuiz.rationale: The partitions are below 5, 5–20 and above 20. The correct set has one representative in each; the distractors omit one or two partitions.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Two independent inputs each have three partitions. Each Choice is required, not combinations. What is the minimum number of cases if every combination is feasible?
practiceQuiz.rationale: Three cases can pair corresponding partitions so each input's three partitions appear. Nine is all combinations; six unnecessarily separates inputs; one misses partitions.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A numeric age field accepts all integers as possible inputs, accepts 18–65 inclusive as valid, and rejects other integers. Which is the exact minimum 2-value BVA coverage-item set across all partitions?
practiceQuiz.rationale: The finite boundaries of the three partitions are 17,18,65,66. They form the full 2-value set. Full 3-value coverage would add 16,19,64,67; testing just six values is incomplete for that stronger criterion.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Text length has feasible domain 0,1,2,...; lengths 10–30 are valid and all other feasible lengths are rejected. Which set achieves full 3-value BVA across all partitions?
practiceQuiz.rationale: The partition boundaries are 0,9,10,30,31. Take each boundary and both immediate feasible neighbors, then deduplicate: 0,1,8,9,10,11,29,30,31,32. The outer boundary contributes 0 and 1; negative lengths are infeasible.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A discount requires member AND basketHigh. A full decision table has four feasible rules. Tests cover (true,true), (true,false) and (false,true). Which additional case completes rule coverage with the correct expected result?
practiceQuiz.rationale: Enumerate the four condition combinations. The missing rule is false/false and cannot satisfy AND, so no discount is expected. Giving a discount violates the rule; repeating true/true or true/false adds no coverage.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Coupons may be issued only to members. A discount requires member AND coupon. The combination member=false,coupon=true is therefore infeasible. Existing tests cover false/false and true/true. Which added test completes feasible-rule coverage?
practiceQuiz.rationale: After removing the infeasible false/true combination, three rules remain. True/false is missing and should not receive a discount. An infeasible combination cannot close a feasible-rule gap; true/true is already covered.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A model has transitions A→B, B→C and B→A. A test follows A→B→C. What valid transition coverage is achieved?
practiceQuiz.rationale: The test exercises A→B and B→C but misses B→A. Visiting every state does not guarantee every transition.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Initial state is Draft. Submit moves to Pending; approve moves Pending to Approved; cancel moves Draft to Closed. Which sequence is valid?
practiceQuiz.rationale: Submit then approve follows defined transitions. Other sequences attempt an event from a state with no matching modeled transition.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A program has 20 executable statements and a suite executes 15. What is statement coverage?
practiceQuiz.rationale: Statement coverage is 15/20×100=75%. The unexecuted fraction is 25%; test count is irrelevant.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: An if-without-else is tested with its condition true, executing every statement. What may still be missing?
practiceQuiz.rationale: Full statement coverage can leave an empty false branch untested. Executed statements and input do not establish decision-outcome coverage.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: What does 100% branch coverage imply for reachable executable statements under the same model?
practiceQuiz.rationale: Branch coverage subsumes statement coverage, not all path combinations or behavioral correctness.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Two independent if decisions have both outcomes covered, but not every outcome combination. What can be true?

options.text: Every path has necessarily been executed
The conditions cannot be tested dynamically
Branch coverage is complete while path coverage is incomplete

practiceQuiz.rationale: Covering each branch does not require every combined route. Statement coverage need not be zero, and the decisions can be dynamically tested.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Coverage is 100% for code that omits a required discount. Which conclusion is sound?

options.text: Full code coverage proves all requirements are implemented
Specification-based tests are needed to expose the missing behavior
Coverage tools automatically supply omitted business rules
The missing discount cannot be a defect

practiceQuiz.rationale: Coverage measures implemented structure. It cannot establish that absent required code exists or derive missing business rules by itself.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Why add structural coverage measurement to behavior-based tests?

options.text: It can reveal implemented code not exercised by the suite
It replaces the need to define expected outputs
It guarantees that all paths are feasible

practiceQuiz.rationale: Coverage highlights structural gaps. It does not provide an oracle, guarantee path feasibility or replace acceptance evidence.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Prior incidents involved leap-day dates. A tester targets those dates in a new release. Which technique is this?
practiceQuiz.rationale: The test choice comes from knowledge of prior mistakes. No structural or partition/table model is specified.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: What makes error guessing more systematic?

options.text: Organizing likely fault types and corresponding attacks
Restricting tests to already passing scripts

practiceQuiz.rationale: A fault-attack list turns experience into targeted tests. Randomness and ignoring defect history do not support this technique.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A tester learns from an unexpected result and immediately designs a follow-up within a charter. Which technique fits?
practiceQuiz.rationale: Exploration integrates learning, design and execution. The alternatives either fix the sequence or address different activities.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: What best supports a repeatable account of an exploratory session?

options.text: A claim that no planning is permitted
An instruction to click freely without notes
A charter, timebox, observations and debrief

practiceQuiz.rationale: Session structure and recorded evidence support accountability. Random clicking and invented coverage do not.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A tester uses a list of accessibility conditions but chooses screen-specific steps. Which technique fits?
practiceQuiz.rationale: A checklist states what to check while allowing tailored execution. It need not prescribe every step or examine internal code structure.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Repeated incidents reveal a condition absent from the checklist. What should happen?

options.text: Assume that an unlisted condition is outside quality scope
Evaluate and update the checklist to cover the relevant risk
Keep the list fixed to preserve historical comparability

practiceQuiz.rationale: Checklist quality depends on relevant learning. Updating it is more appropriate than freezing it, discarding useful coverage or ignoring the risk.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Business, development and testing discuss a story's edge cases. What is the main benefit?

options.text: Transferring quality responsibility to business staff
Removing the need for acceptance criteria

practiceQuiz.rationale: Collaboration exposes ambiguity and aligns expectations. Criteria and shared responsibility remain; a story is negotiable.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which story violates the Testable part of INVEST most clearly?

options.text: As a user, I want an amazingly intuitive screen
As a member, I want to reset my expired password
As a clerk, I want to export a selected invoice
As a buyer, I want to filter by an available size

practiceQuiz.rationale: A subjective adjective without observable criteria is hard to test. The other stories describe observable capabilities, although they still need refinement.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Acceptance criteria are written as Given/When/Then examples. Which format is this?
practiceQuiz.rationale: Given/When/Then describes a scenario. A rule list is rule-oriented; the other labels do not describe these acceptance formats.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A list states allowable file types and maximum sizes. Which acceptance format most naturally fits?
practiceQuiz.rationale: A verification list of constraints is rule-oriented. It can be translated into scenarios but is not inherently a runtime sequence or defect workflow.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Free delivery applies to integer basket totals of at least EUR 50. Which pair checks the threshold correctly?
practiceQuiz.rationale: At least 50 includes 50 and excludes 49. The distractors contradict the specified inclusive threshold.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A story locks an account on the third consecutive failed login. Initially the failure count is zero. Which test best follows the criterion?

options.text: Fail once, then require password deletion
Fail twice, then require a locked account
Fail three times, then verify the account is locked
Succeed once, then require a locked account

practiceQuiz.rationale: The third consecutive failure triggers locking. Earlier locking or deletion invents behavior not stated in the acceptance rule.
practiceQuiz.hint: Identify the objective and apply the decision rule to the facts before comparing alternatives.

quickRecap.value: Black-box techniques model specified behavior; white-box techniques analyze internal structure; experience-based techniques exploit tester knowledge. They complement each other rather than competing for a universal best choice.

Identify non-empty, non-overlapping groups expected to be treated alike. Cover valid and invalid partitions. Each Choice for multiple inputs covers every partition of each input, not every combination.

Start with the feasible input domain and every ordered partition, including invalid partitions. List each finite minimum and maximum. The union of these boundary values is the 2-value coverage set. For 3-value coverage add both immediate neighbors of every boundary value, keep only feasible inputs and deduplicate. An unbounded integer domain with accepted L through U has finite boundaries L-1,L,U,U+1; full 3-value coverage normally also needs L-2,L+1,U-1,U+2. A bounded domain can add outer endpoints and their feasible neighbors; close boundaries can overlap.

Represent condition combinations as rules and associate actions. Remove infeasible rules; merge rules with identical outcomes when a condition is irrelevant. Coverage counts exercised feasible rules, not individual conditions.

Model states and event-triggered transitions, including guards and actions. State coverage can miss transitions. All valid transition coverage exercises each modeled valid transition. All transitions coverage adds attempted invalid transitions from the state table; isolate one invalid transition per test to avoid defect masking. All transitions coverage subsumes valid transitions coverage, which subsumes all states coverage.
Statement coverage is executed executable statements divided by total executable statements. Full statement coverage says nothing certain about untested decision outcomes or missing requirements.
Branch coverage counts exercised control-flow branches. Full branch coverage subsumes full statement coverage, but not the reverse; neither implies all paths or correct requirements.
Structural coverage supplies objective evidence and can reveal gaps in behavior-based testing. It cannot identify an omitted requirement simply because all implemented code is exercised.
Use experience of errors, defects, failures and the application domain to target likely mistakes. Fault attacks organize likely defect types and corresponding tests.

Learning, test design and execution influence each other during exploration. A timeboxed session can use a charter, notes, coverage observations and a debrief; exploration is not unrecorded random clicking.

Use a list of conditions derived from experience and needs to guide checks. Keep it relevant and update it with findings. Broad items permit varied execution, but vague or stale lists can miss defects.

Business, development and testing perspectives refine a story together. The card starts a conversation and confirmation examples clarify intent. INVEST asks for independent, negotiable, valuable, estimable, small and testable stories.
Acceptance criteria set shared, unambiguous conditions for accepting a story and include positive and negative behavior. They may be scenario-oriented or rule-oriented.

Discuss the story and criteria before implementation; derive stakeholder-readable tests for its characteristics. Include positive, negative and relevant non-functional cases without inventing unrelated scope. Agree concrete examples before implementation, then use their expected results to guide the work.
